chunks: "There are four main families. A through via goes all the way from the top to the bottom layer.
It's the cheapest, because it's one drilling and plating step for the whole board, but it takes space on every layer and leaves a stub on a fast signal that exits early.
A blind via starts on an outer layer and stops at an inner one, so it doesn't use the layers below it.
A buried via connects inner layers and never reaches the surface, which frees the outer layers completely.
And a microvia is a very small laser-drilled blind via, usually spanning just one layer, and it's what lets you escape fine-pitch BGAs. Microvias can be stacked or staggered.
The tradeoffs are mostly cost versus density. Blind and buried vias need sequential lamination, so extra press cycles, extra drilling and plating steps, and more yield risk.
Microvias need laser equipment and an HDI process. In return you get routing density and short stubs.
The default is through vias, and I only go to the others when the BGA pitch, the layer count or signal integrity forces it.
I'd also talk to the fab about their capabilities before choosing, because aspect ratio and stacking limits vary."
